analysis.one_liner: Sets minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios in every hospital, including those paid by Medicare.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 45 House sponsors but never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 109th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would require hospitals to staff each unit with no more than a set number of patients per direct-care registered nurse — one nurse per patient in trauma and operating rooms, up to six in well-baby nurseries. Hospitals would have to build staffing plans with input from nurses, post actual staffing levels for the public, keep records, and face federal audits. Nurses could refuse assignments that violate the ratios or that they are not trained for, and hospitals could not punish them for refusing or for reporting violations.
analysis.who_benefits: Hospital patients, who get safer staffing levels linked in studies to fewer preventable injuries and deaths, and nurses, who get limits on how many patients they can be assigned at once, a right to refuse unsafe assignments, and legal protection against retaliation.

how_it_helps.text: Caps how many patients one direct-care registered nurse can be assigned per shift, ranging from 1:1 in operating and trauma emergency units to 1:6 in postpartum and well-baby units, with stricter limits possible through federal regulation.

Requires hospitals to develop staffing plans with input from the nurses themselves, post actual nurse-to-patient ratios in each unit where staff, patients, and the public can see them, keep three years of records, and undergo periodic audits by the Health and Human Services Department.

Gives nurses the right to refuse an assignment that would violate the staffing rules or that they lack the training to handle safely, bars hospitals from firing, disciplining, or reporting them to licensing boards for refusing, and creates a federal court cause of action with reinstatement, back pay, and attorneys' fees.

Requires Medicare to adjust hospital payments to cover the net added costs of compliance, so hospitals that follow the staffing rules would not absorb the full expense — and gives rural hospitals four years instead of two to meet the ratios.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, which must hire more nurses and run units at ratios that raise payroll costs, though Medicare payment adjustments would shift much of that expense to federal spending, and ultimately taxpayers, who fund Medicare.

drawbacks.text: The bill orders Medicare to pay hospitals the net additional costs of compliance, so a large share of the cost of safer staffing would land on the Medicare program and taxpayers rather than on hospital margins.

Fixed numeric ratios are a blunt tool: hospitals would still have to find nurses in a workforce that was already short-handed, and critics of ratio mandates argue that rigid headcounts, even with acuity adjustments, reduce flexibility for unusual shifts and could strain smaller and rural facilities — which is why the bill gives rural hospitals double the phase-in time.
All staffing requirements are suspended during a declared state of emergency, so the protections would not apply in exactly the surge situations where staffing is most stressed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The patient-safety benefit is the core of the bill and is backed by the research it cites, and the nurse-protection provisions are unusually concrete (a real court remedy, not just a rule). The honest cost is fiscal: by reimbursing hospitals through Medicare, the bill spreads the expense to taxpayers instead of making hospital budgets absorb it, and the phase-in schedules recognize that a national nurse shortage limits how fast ratios can be met. A reasonable design trade-off, though one that shifts a real bill to the public purse.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means committees and then to their Health subcommittees in March 2005, and neither panel ever took it up before the Congress ended in January 2007.

narrative.text: Rep. Janice Schakowsky introduced the Nurse Staffing Standards for Patient Safety and Quality Care Act on March 10, 2005, with 15 original cosponsors, and 44 members total signed on — all Democrats or the chamber's one Independent.

The bill was referred to two committees, Energy and Commerce and Ways and Means, and within days was sent to the Health subcommittees of both, where it stayed for the rest of the 109th Congress with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote.

The bill text required Medicare to adjust hospital payments to cover compliance costs and let the Medicare Payment Advisory Commission estimate the total cost before adjustments took effect, meaning the fiscal question was designed to be answered rather than avoided.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals that would have faced mandatory hiring and higher payroll costs came out ahead, along with the federal Medicare budget, which avoided the payment adjustments. Patients kept the staffing levels the bill found to contribute to preventable injuries and deaths.

for.name: Rep. Janice Schakowsky
for.role: Sponsor, House Energy and Commerce Committee member
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 44 cosponsors for a national version of California-style nurse staffing ratios.

for.name: 43 of 202 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; every Democratic cosponsor the bill attracted was a Democrat, plus the chamber's one Independent.

for.name: American Nurses Association
for.role: National nurses' union and professional association
for.what_they_did: Publicly backed federal minimum nurse-to-patient staffing ratios, building on the campaign that won California's staffing law.

against.name: Rep. Joe Barton
against.role: Chair, House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for a markup or a floor vote while chairing the primary committee of jurisdiction.

against.name: Rep. Bill Thomas
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration in the second committee of referral, which controlled its Medicare payment provisions.

against.name: Hospital industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed mandated nurse-to-patient ratios, arguing they would raise labor costs and reduce staffing flexibility; the industry had fought the same requirement in California.

sides.party_line_note: All 44 cosponsors were Democrats or the chamber's one Independent; no Republican signed on, and the two Republican committee chairs who controlled the bill's path took no action on it.

industries.note: The bill forces hospitals to hire more direct-care nurses and post their staffing levels publicly, raising payroll costs and reducing their ability to run units lean. But it orders Medicare to pay hospitals the net added cost of compliance, so much of the expense would flow back to them through federal reimbursements. Their interest in avoiding the mandate runs against the patient-safety goal it serves.

industries.industry: Registered nurses and bedside nursing workforce
industries.note: Nurses get enforceable limits on patient assignments, a right to refuse unsafe assignments, and anti-retaliation protection with a court remedy. The bill's own findings argue the ratios would also improve recruitment and retention of nurses.

The bill directs Medicare to adjust hospital payments to cover the net additional compliance costs and authorizes appropriations for federally operated hospitals, so the federal budget absorbs a substantial share of the price of safer staffing.
